title: Households interpret monetary tightening through expected costs and inflation
source_unit: US household survey respondent with randomized hypothetical-rate and information treatments

denominator.unit: retained US residents ages 25–70 after quality and plausibility filters

survey_design.value: quota-based online survey with weights matching age, gender, and region; respondents report consumption, expectations, debt, assets, and policy responses

follow_up_wave.unit: first-wave respondents participating in February 9–21, 2025 follow-up

observations.method: Large-scale Cint household survey with demographic quotas, survey weights, hypothetical federal-funds-rate scenarios, randomized information treatments, and a three-month follow-up.
observations.uncertainty: The online quota sample is weighted to selected demographics but is not a simple random sample. Several reported measures are hypothetical or intended behavior; cleaning rules replace extreme responses with missing values, and the follow-up is smaller.
observations.subgroup: US residents ages 25–70; study also reports heterogeneity by age, gender, income, education, debt, wealth, financial literacy, and Federal Reserve knowledge.
observations.counterinterpretation: Reported expectations and intended actions may not become realized spending, debt, employment, or portfolio changes; demographic weighting does not remove nonresponse, selection, or comprehension differences.

denominator.unit: first-wave survey respondents; regression-specific valid universes may be smaller

overall_spending.unit: percentage-point change in reported spending response per 1 percentage-point FFR increase

durable_goods_spending.unit: percentage-point change in reported durable-goods spending response per 1 percentage-point FFR increase

observations.method: Weighted Huber-adjusted regression of hypothetical spending response on randomized hypothetical FFR change, with demographic and socioeconomic controls.
observations.uncertainty: The effects are economically small, hypothetical, and regression-specific; the overall estimate is reported as less than 0.1 percentage point in the paper text. This is not an observed contract-rate or transaction response.
observations.subgroup: All valid first-wave respondents, with heterogeneity by financial literacy, Federal Reserve knowledge, income, education, debt, and other characteristics.
observations.counterinterpretation: Respondents may understand or answer hypothetical policy questions differently from how they act when a real rate changes; borrowers, savers, renters, and owners face different pass-through.

observations.period: 2024 randomized information treatment and three-month follow-up

denominator.unit: follow-up respondents participating in both survey waves; treatment-specific valid universes vary

durable_spending_pass_through.unit: percentage-point change in durable consumption per 1 percentage-point higher-than-expected FFR information surprise among financially literate/Fed-knowledgeable respondents

rate-cut_durable_spending.unit: percentage-point increase in durable consumption per 1 percentage-point lower-than-expected FFR information surprise

follow_up_scale.unit: approximate percent of hypothetical-scenario sample represented by randomized information-treatment follow-up analysis

observations.method: Randomized information about the federal funds rate, comparison of prior beliefs with post-treatment expectations, and regression of three-month spending change on positive or negative forecast surprises; sampling weights and controls used.
observations.uncertainty: The randomized information result has lower precision because the follow-up is much smaller than the hypothetical sample. The durable-spending estimate is a partial-equilibrium, short-horizon treatment result and not a full macroeconomic rate-shock estimate.
observations.subgroup: Especially financially literate respondents who recognize the Federal Reserve's role; the paper reports weaker or imprecise responses among other respondents.
observations.counterinterpretation: The treatment may change reported expectations without changing durable purchases for many households; observed responses can depend on liquidity, existing contracts, and the timing of a purchase.

denominator.unit: first-wave survey respondents; instrument-specific valid universes vary

inflation_expectations_channel.value: predominant relative to other measured expectations in the paper's decomposition
inflation_expectations_channel.unit: relative contribution to perceived spending response

income_expectations.value: FFR changes have little effect on expected income

portfolio_direction.value: higher perceived rates shift intended allocation away from stocks toward bank deposits

observations.method: Consumption and portfolio equations using randomized information treatments as instruments for revisions in inflation, income, rates, asset prices, and other expectations.
observations.uncertainty: The decomposition identifies treatment-induced expectation pass-through within the survey design; it is not a complete general-equilibrium estimate and does not measure actual realized portfolios for every respondent.
observations.subgroup: Survey respondents with reported financial, demographic, and political characteristics; subgroup effects vary by financial knowledge and household position.
observations.counterinterpretation: The cost-channel interpretation may reflect the survey framing or contemporaneous macro context; other households may respond through income, credit access, housing, or employment channels not dominant in this design.

related_sources.claim: NBER Working Paper 35127 record for the same study and authors.

boundary: This record measures household perceptions, intended responses, randomized information effects, and expectation channels around hypothetical or perceived federal-funds-rate changes. It does not establish the general-equilibrium effect of an actual rate decision, realized household spending or portfolios for all respondents, effects on trust or voting, or a causal cultural or political response. The source is a BIS working paper and the survey is quota-based online data; preserve its draft and sampling boundaries.
